Outcome_variable.evidence_source: [/page/1/Text/11] Previous research has tested social reactivity and social participation using daily diary methods, in which participants described their daily activities and how happy they felt during those activities. Despite these preliminary findings for extraversion and positive affect, neither the social participation hypothesis nor the social reactivity hypotheses have been examined in relation to more stable assessments such as life satisfaction. Life satisfaction makes up the cognitive component of subjective well-being; it is not a feeling but rather a judgement based on the state of one's life (Diener, Oishi, & Lucas, 2003a).
